view.stem: Use an ideal infinitely long straight-wire model: positive ions are at rest and electrons drift uniformly along the wire at a nonzero speed. In the ion-rest frame, the positive and negative line-charge densities cancel, the exterior electric field is zero, and the current is steady and nonzero. There are no other fields. Change only the observer's inertial frame, not the wire model. Which statement about the fields throughout the exterior space around the wire is valid?

options.text: A frame moving with the electrons makes the magnetic field zero everywhere; the electric field need not be zero.
A frame moving with the positive ions makes the magnetic field zero everywhere; the electric field need not be zero.
No inertial frame makes the magnetic field zero everywhere; the electric field may change with the frame.
An inertial frame exists that makes both the electric and magnetic fields zero everywhere.

intent.task: For the explicitly specified neutral steady straight-wire model, decide whether an inertial change of frame can eliminate the magnetic field throughout the exterior, rather than merely recognize an examination principle.
intent.source_solution: The original open source still requires a charge/current/frame model and does not permit a universal unconditional outcome. The choice visibly selects an ideal infinite neutral wire with steady current and no other fields as a comparison model. In the ion-rest frame, exterior E=0 and B=mu0*I/(2*pi*r) is nonzero at every finite exterior distance r>0. For any subluminal inertial boost, decompose B parallel and perpendicular to the relative velocity. Field transformations give B'_parallel=B_parallel and B'_perpendicular=gamma*B_perpendicular. A nonzero B cannot have both orthogonal components become zero. Therefore no inertial frame eliminates B throughout the exterior. Moving with the electrons leaves moving positive ions; moving with the ions leaves current-carrying electrons. This result is not generalized to every charged conductor and does not require an unchanged electric field.
intent.unit_reason: One single question compares the specified model's complete field-removal outcome with the two population-rest inferences and a simultaneous-two-field-removal claim. The learner must choose an actual regional field result for that model.
limitations: The visible model fixes an infinite neutral steady straight wire and inertial frames, excluding other charge models, end effects and non-inertial frames.
Recognizing the specified model's field result does not demonstrate independent model construction, free field-transformation derivation or classification of all current-carrying conductors.
Freely enumerating missing conditions for an unspecified model remains an uncovered open-expression capacity.

rationales.derivation: When the electrons are at rest, the positive ions move relative to the observer. For an axial boost the initial B is perpendicular to the velocity, and E=0 gives B'=gamma*B, still nonzero. One cannot keep only resting electrons and discard the moving ions.
rationales.misconception: Treat only electron drift current as the total magnetic source, set that current to zero in the electron-rest frame and omit the now-moving positive ions.

rationales.derivation: The ion-rest frame is the frame specified in the stem. Electrons still drift at nonzero speed, so the current and B=mu0*I/(2*pi*r) are nonzero at every finite exterior distance.
rationales.misconception: Equate rest of the wire and positive ions with rest of every conductor charge, omitting the drifting-electron current.

rationales.derivation: With E=0, any inertial boost retains the parallel B component and multiplies the perpendicular component by nonzero gamma. It cannot eliminate a nonzero B, and therefore cannot eliminate B throughout the exterior. E' can arise after a boost; the argument does not assume individually invariant field components.
Eliminating both fields everywhere would in particular eliminate B everywhere, which no inertial boost can do for the stated model. Thus no such frame exists.
rationales.misconception: Mistake macroscopic neutrality for absence of all electromagnetic sources, then assume a change of observer can remove both the moving-charge magnetic field and every electric field.

view.stem: Model the fixed transmitting and receiving devices as ideal short straight electric dipole oscillators, considering only the direct far field in free space. The transmitter oscillates with nonzero amplitude. Their axes are perpendicular, but the direction joining the devices has not been specified. Which statements about the drive of the receiving oscillator are valid?

options.text: The field direction at the receiver depends only on the transmitting axis, not on the direction joining the devices.
The receiver's axial drive is determined by the incident electric field component along its axis.
Perpendicular axes are sufficient to establish zero axial drive in the receiving oscillator.
Keeping the axes perpendicular while changing the joining direction may change the field component along the receiving axis.

intent.task: Within the visibly stated ideal direct-far-field model, distinguish the angle between oscillator axes, propagation direction and the incident field projection along the receiving axis, leaving the actual joining direction unresolved.
intent.source_solution: The source oscillator model and relative spatial placement are incomplete, so mutual perpendicularity does not give a universal reception result. As an explicitly named comparison model, the direct far field of an ideal short electric dipole has E proportional to p-n(n dot p), and receiver axial drive is proportional to r dot E, with p and r the transmitting and receiving axes and n the propagation direction. Perpendicular axes give r dot p=0, but the remaining -(r dot n)(p dot n) still varies with joining direction. Directions perpendicular to an axis and directions with components along both axes give different coupling; these are dependence tests, not an undisclosed actual arrangement. The general source may also discuss other oscillator models, near fields or reflection.
intent.unit_reason: One multiple question judges radiation direction and receiving projection together. It is not split into unconditional reception/non-reception clicks and does not ask the learner to guess an actual spatial layout.
limitations: The visible stem specifies fixed ideal short straight electric dipoles, nonzero transmitted oscillation and the free-space direct far field.
Other oscillator models, near fields, reflections and non-ideal receiving responses are not covered.
Recognition does not demonstrate independently choosing and drawing an arrangement, solving it fully or freely stating every applicability condition.
The actual joining direction remains unspecified; the choice key cannot be interpreted as a universal yes/no for the unresolved source arrangement.

rationales.derivation: The ideal dipole far field is the transmitting-axis projection onto the plane perpendicular to propagation: E proportional to p-n(n dot p). Changing n changes that projection, so E is not generally parallel to p.
rationales.misconception: Copy the charge-oscillation direction into the electric field at every observing direction, omitting the transverse projection.

rationales.derivation: In the visibly specified ideal short straight electric-dipole model, the axial electric force drives the charges. It is proportional to the incident electric field component along the receiving axis, including the case where that component is zero.

For a test of necessity, take p along z and r along x, and compare n along y with n along (x+z)/sqrt(2). The first gives r dot E=0; the second is proportional to -1/2. Both keep the axes perpendicular, so the axis angle alone does not establish zero drive. These directions are counterexample calculations, not hidden actual positions.
rationales.misconception: Use r dot p=0 to infer zero, incorrectly identify the receiver's electric field E with p, and omit the propagation-dependent projection term.

rationales.derivation: With fixed perpendicular axes, r dot E is proportional to -(r dot n)(p dot n). Changing n while retaining a far-field distance can change that product, so the axial component may change. This does not claim that every change of direction must change it.

view.stem: In the radio receiver shown, the tuning coil has inductance $L=2\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{H}$, and the variable capacitor's capacitance $C$ can vary continuously from $12$ to $450\,\mathrm{pF}$, including both endpoints. Use the ideal LC resonance model, neglecting parasitic capacitance and the detector section's effect on tuning, and take the electromagnetic-wave speed as $c=3.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Which option correctly gives the complete tunable wavelength range and the capacitances corresponding to the shortest and longest wavelengths? Round wavelengths to one decimal place.

options.text: The wavelength range is approximately $14.7$ to $90.0\,\mathrm{m}$; the shortest wavelength corresponds to $C=12\,\mathrm{pF}$, and the longest to $C=450\,\mathrm{pF}$.
The wavelength range is approximately $92.3$ to $565.5\,\mathrm{m}$; the shortest wavelength corresponds to $C=450\,\mathrm{pF}$, and the longest to $C=12\,\mathrm{pF}$.
The wavelength range is approximately $92.3$ to $3462.9\,\mathrm{m}$; the shortest wavelength corresponds to $C=12\,\mathrm{pF}$, and the longest to $C=450\,\mathrm{pF}$.
The wavelength range is approximately $92.3$ to $565.5\,\mathrm{m}$; the shortest wavelength corresponds to $C=12\,\mathrm{pF}$, and the longest to $C=450\,\mathrm{pF}$.

intent.task: Determine the full tuning-wavelength interval of an ideal LC receiver with fixed inductance and variable capacitance, convert pF to F, and assign the two capacitance endpoints to the shortest and longest wavelengths. The task is not one wavelength at an arbitrary capacitance or a sequence of numerical blanks.
intent.source_solution: Solved independently before alternatives: an ideal LC circuit obeys Lq''+q/C=0, giving angular frequency omega_0=1/sqrt(LC) and ordinary frequency f_0=1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)). Resonant tuning requires the incident frequency to equal f_0, so lambda=c/f_0=2 pi c sqrt(LC). Convert 12 pF to 1.2e-11 F and 450 pF to 4.5e-10 F. With L=2e-4 H and c=3e8 m/s, the endpoint wavelengths are 12 pi sqrt(6) m=92.34358777165421 m and 180 pi m=565.4866776461628 m. Since lambda increases continuously and strictly with positive C, the full closed interval is [12 pi sqrt(6),180 pi] m, approximately 92.3 to 565.5 m; 12 pF gives the shortest wavelength and 450 pF the longest. The brackets include the exact attainable endpoints; displayed decimals are rounded. Necessary conditions are that the given C is the effective tuning capacitance, L is fixed, loss/parasitic capacitance/detector loading are neglected, and the specified wave speed is used. The separate right-hand detector capacitor is not added to C. This is an ideal tuning range, not a guarantee of sufficiently strong broadcasts at every wavelength.
intent.unit_reason: A complete wavelength interval together with its capacitance-endpoint mapping is one coherent tuning-range judgment, so one native single-choice item is appropriate. Each of the four alternatives is a complete individually testable result and exactly one is true. The endpoints are not split into arithmetic clicks, and the alternatives are not combination codes.
limitations: Selecting a complete correct result cannot establish unaided production of the LC formula, SI conversion and numerical working.
Endpoint correspondence is still tested, but selection cannot establish unaided written explanations of wavelength monotonicity and the resonance condition.

Since lambda increases continuously and strictly for positive C, 12 pF gives the shortest wavelength and 450 pF the longest, with both endpoints attainable. Rounding as requested gives 92.3 m and 565.5 m.

view.stem: The figure shows a television receiving antenna. Which judgments about the station's wave are valid? Only when an option explicitly adds assumptions should the horizontal crossbar be treated as the effective receiving axis of an ideal electric dipole and a nonzero far-field free-space plane-wave model be used. For conditional discussion, introduce a right-handed orthonormal basis: $\hat{\mathbf x}$ runs along the horizontal crossbar, $\hat{\mathbf z}$ points vertically upward, and $\hat{\mathbf y}$ is horizontal with $\hat{\mathbf x}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=\hat{\mathbf z}$; $\hat{\mathbf n}$ denotes the wave's propagation direction. These coordinates and models are assumptions for discussion, not measurements from the figure. Select all valid judgments.

options.text: The antenna's appearance alone does not uniquely determine the incident wave's magnetic-field oscillation direction; further inference from the antenna requires stated incident-wave, propagation and reception-matching conditions.

If the wave is additionally assumed to be linearly polarized with its electric field along $\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\hat{\mathbf n}=\hat{\mathbf y}$, its magnetic field oscillates back and forth along a vertical axis parallel to $\hat{\mathbf z}$.

If the wave is additionally assumed to be linearly polarized with its electric field along $\hat{\mathbf x}$ but $\hat{\mathbf n}=(\hat{\mathbf y}+\hat{\mathbf z})/\sqrt{2}$, its magnetic field oscillates back and forth along a tilted axis parallel to $(\hat{\mathbf y}-\hat{\mathbf z})/\sqrt{2}$.

If the wave is additionally assumed to be linearly polarized with its electric field along $\hat{\mathbf x}$ while $\hat{\mathbf n}=\hat{\mathbf x}$, it can still be a wave satisfying this model and be fully polarization-matched to the horizontal crossbar.

intent.task: Separate visible evidence from added model assumptions and judge the magnetic-field direction or feasibility of horizontal, oblique and along-rod propagation under full linear polarization alignment. Preserve the source's conditional magnetic-field discussion instead of treating a horizontal antenna silhouette as unconditional evidence of vertical B.
intent.source_solution: Solved independently after reading both source-4 seeds and actually viewing the complete Figure 127 rendering, before constructing alternatives. The figure provides no propagation vector, E/B arrows or polarization/matching data, so it does not uniquely fix the B oscillation axis. Conditionally adopt a far-field free-space plane wave and ideal electric dipole with rod axis a=x: E is perpendicular to propagation n, B=n cross E/c, and receiving voltage is proportional to a dot E. Full linear alignment E parallel x is feasible only for n perpendicular x. For n=y, y cross x=-z gives vertical oscillation. For n=(y+z)/sqrt(2), n cross x=(y-z)/sqrt(2) gives a tilted axis. For n=x, nonzero E parallel x violates transversality. Further, with n=y, linear E proportional to (x+z)/sqrt(2) has a receiving component but tilted B along (x-z)/sqrt(2); circular E=E0[x cos(phi)+z sin(phi)] also has a receiving component while B rotates in the xz plane. These are explicitly conditional examples, not identifications of the pictured station's wave. The full pre-option derivation and actual-image evidence are in report.md.
intent.unit_reason: Use one native multiple item to judge the figure's information boundary and three physical assertions under different propagation conditions. Changing propagation direction and testing a longitudinal-field assumption are this item's independent reasoning unit. The other item examines specific imperfectly matched polarizations and receiver response, not this information-boundary or propagation-geometry task.

The spatial B axis depends on missing conditions. Conditional receivable waves with tilted or rotating B exist, so appearance cannot uniquely determine B.

The added assumptions give E parallel x and n=y. The free-space plane-wave relation B=n cross E/c and y cross x=-z yield oscillation along the vertical line. The minus sign specifies direction at one phase, not a different axis or a permanently downward field.

The stated n=(y+z)/sqrt(2) remains perpendicular to E parallel x, so the model is consistent. Compute n cross x=(y cross x+z cross x)/sqrt(2)=(-z+y)/sqrt(2). This axis has both horizontal and vertical components and is tilted rather than vertical; the signed linear field alternates with phase.

view.stem: To discuss waves the pictured antenna can receive, additionally model its horizontal crossbar using ideal electric-dipole polarization coupling, ignoring noise, attenuation and detector thresholds. Choose a right-handed orthonormal basis with $\hat{\mathbf x}$ along the crossbar, $\hat{\mathbf z}$ vertically upward and $\hat{\mathbf x}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=\hat{\mathbf z}$. Compare two far-field free-space plane waves propagating along $+\hat{\mathbf y}$, with electric fields $\mathbf E_I=E_0\cos\varphi\,(\hat{\mathbf x}+\hat{\mathbf z})/\sqrt{2}$ and $\mathbf E_{II}=E_0(\hat{\mathbf x}\cos\varphi+\hat{\mathbf z}\sin\varphi)$, where $E_0>0$, $\varphi=ky-\omega t$, $\omega=ck>0$ and $c$ is wave speed. These are hypothetical incident waves, not fields measured from the figure. Which option correctly describes each wave's magnetic-field behavior and whether it produces an alternating receiving voltage that is not identically zero?

options.text: Wave $I$: an alternating voltage is produced, and $\mathbf B$ oscillates along an axis parallel to $(\hat{\mathbf x}-\hat{\mathbf z})/\sqrt{2}$. Wave $II$: an alternating voltage is produced, and $\mathbf B$ oscillates along an axis parallel to $\hat{\mathbf z}$.

Wave $I$: no alternating voltage is produced, and $\mathbf B$ oscillates along an axis parallel to $(\hat{\mathbf x}-\hat{\mathbf z})/\sqrt{2}$. Wave $II$: no alternating voltage is produced, and $\mathbf B$ rotates in the $xz$ plane.

Wave $I$: an alternating voltage is produced, and $\mathbf B$ oscillates along an axis parallel to $(\hat{\mathbf x}-\hat{\mathbf z})/\sqrt{2}$. Wave $II$: an alternating voltage is produced, and $\mathbf B$ rotates in the $xz$ plane.

Wave $I$: an alternating voltage is produced, and $\mathbf B$ oscillates along an axis parallel to $(\hat{\mathbf x}+\hat{\mathbf z})/\sqrt{2}$. Wave $II$: an alternating voltage is produced, and $\mathbf B$ rotates in the $xz$ plane.

intent.task: For two explicitly specified hypothetical incident waves, distinguish tilted linear magnetic-field oscillation from rotation in a plane and determine whether a horizontal electric dipole has alternating voltage response. Use concrete tilted-linear and circular polarization examples to separate reception from full polarization matching and substantively explain why reception does not unconditionally imply vertical B in the source problem.
intent.source_solution: The original image has no measured incident-wave polarization, propagation direction or matching data and cannot uniquely identify the real B. In the explicitly hypothetical far-field free-space plane-wave and ideal electric-dipole polarization model, the rod axis is x and propagation n=y. B=y cross E/c, while alternating receiving voltage is proportional to x dot E. Wave I has E=E0 cos(phi)(x+z)/sqrt(2), hence B_I=(E0/c)cos(phi)(x-z)/sqrt(2) and voltage proportional to E0 cos(phi)/sqrt(2): tilted linear B and a non-identically-zero alternating response. Wave II has E=E0[x cos(phi)+z sin(phi)], hence B_II=(E0/c)[x sin(phi)-z cos(phi)] and voltage proportional to E0 cos(phi): rotating B in the xz plane and a non-identically-zero alternating response. Neither requires E to remain wholly aligned with the rod; measuring one component does not project the incident wave into another polarization. Zero voltage at individual phases is not identically zero alternating response. These are conditional counterexamples, not assertions about the real station's transmitted polarization. The full derivation was recorded before alternatives in report.md.
intent.unit_reason: Use one native single item for a complete magnetic-field/receiver comparison of the two polarizations; exactly one complete result is correct. It requires specific vector reasoning, distinction between linear and rotating polarization, and distinction between a nonzero component and optimum matching. It does not repeat an insufficient-information choice or reuse the other item's perfectly aligned horizontal or oblique-propagation answers.
limitations: Selecting the complete field/receiver result does not demonstrate unaided construction of counterexamples or production of cross-product/component working.
Alternating voltage under ideal polarization coupling does not guarantee usable television reception with noise, attenuation or detector thresholds; the real station's polarization is not inferred.

rationales.derivation: Wave I is described correctly. For wave II, first projecting E onto the rod retains only E0 cos(phi)x; then applying y cross E/c incorrectly yields B only along -z. The actual wave retains E0 sin(phi)z, which contributes (E0/c)sin(phi)x to the cross product. Thus B rotates rather than oscillating along a fixed z line.
rationales.misconception: Replace the full incident electric field by the antenna-detected projection, discard wave II's z component before computing B, and turn circular polarization into rod-aligned linear polarization.

rationales.derivation: Both magnetic-field behaviors are correct, but reception is misclassified. The along-rod components are E0 cos(phi)/sqrt(2) for wave I and E0 cos(phi) for wave II, neither identically zero. Requiring the complete E direction to align fully with the rod at every phase incorrectly excludes both tilted-linear and circular waves from any alternating response.
rationales.misconception: Treat optimum full polarization matching as necessary for any alternating reception, ignoring that a nonzero along-rod electric-field component already excites an electric dipole.

rationales.derivation: Use y cross x=-z and y cross z=x. Wave I gives B_I=(E0/c)cos(phi)(x-z)/sqrt(2), oscillating along a tilted line. Wave II gives B_II=(E0/c)[x sin(phi)-z cos(phi)], rotating in the xz plane. The rod-axis projections yield voltages proportional to E0 cos(phi)/sqrt(2) and E0 cos(phi), both non-identically-zero alternating responses.

Both voltage responses and wave II's rotation plane are correct, but wave I's B axis is copied from its E axis (x+z)/sqrt(2). The correct cross product yields (x-z)/sqrt(2). Those axes are orthogonal; taking B parallel to E violates the free-space plane-wave field relationship.
rationales.misconception: Copy wave I's electric-polarization axis into its magnetic-field axis, mistaking in-phase electromagnetic variation for spatially parallel fields.

view.stem: Compare radio-wave propagation conditions on the Moon and Earth without assuming a particular band or path. Which statements agree with electromagnetic propagation laws and environmental effects?

options.text: Radio propagation along a vacuum path does not require air as a medium carrying the oscillation.
The same electromagnetic laws make the range of identical equipment independent of band and path at both places.
An Earth ionospheric return path at suitable frequencies cannot be transferred to the Moon without checking the medium.
The Moon's tenuous atmosphere prevents radio waves from propagating along vacuum paths near its surface.

intent.task: Distinguish vacuum electromagnetic propagation, medium-dependent paths and equipment range without asserting equal conditions or no propagation for all terrestrial and lunar bands and paths.
intent.source_solution: Radio waves obey electromagnetic laws and can propagate in vacuum; air is not a required medium. Shared laws do not make terrestrial and lunar environments, all bands and all paths identical. Earth's ionosphere can provide return paths at suitable frequencies, and changes of its state can alter propagation or absorption. The Moon's extremely tenuous exosphere is not an interchangeable terrestrial environment, so the corresponding paths cannot be transferred without checking; a tenuous atmosphere also does not prohibit vacuum radio propagation. Terrain, materials, visibility, frequency and path still affect practical propagation. This item calculates and promises no universal communication range.
intent.unit_reason: One multiple question compares related propagation judgments so that the learner distinguishes law from environment. It does not produce separate unconditional same/different questions for Earth and Moon.
limitations: Recognition does not demonstrate freely writing a complete comparison of terrestrial and lunar propagation environments.
The item tests vacuum medium, ionospheric paths and band/path dependence, not every terrain or material mechanism separately.
The inputs do not support a quantitative link-range comparison for a particular band or path; the draft supplies neither that capacity nor such a conclusion.

rationales.derivation: Radio waves are propagating electromagnetic fields, which can propagate in vacuum. They are not sound waves requiring mechanical oscillations of air particles.

The same electromagnetic laws still allow different media, boundaries and frequencies to produce different paths, absorption and receiving conditions. Identical equipment does not become band/path independent merely because the laws are shared.
rationales.misconception: Eliminate medium, boundary and frequency inputs because the law is the same, and replace that common law with universal equipment performance.

rationales.derivation: Suitable-frequency terrestrial ionospheric paths depend on charged-medium state and density. The Moon has a tenuous exosphere, so shared vacuum electromagnetic propagation does not establish the same return path. The option requires checking the medium; it says neither that all bands return from Earth's ionosphere nor that the Moon has no plasma at all.

A tenuous atmosphere does not remove vacuum electromagnetic propagation. Inferring that radio cannot follow a vacuum path from insufficient air conflicts with the fact that radio needs no supporting air medium.
rationales.misconception: Apply sound's need for a material medium to radio, then turn a tenuous atmosphere into a prohibition on all vacuum radio paths.
